17. **How cities become free.** The ways a city breaks free of its master ("How cities become free"): conquered land not yet absorbed that revolts and breaks free ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice"); a governor who turns with the levies he raised, or a commander who keeps his army, and rules a city of his own, the new Idrimi; and a revolt with no one at its head raising a ruler from its own people ("A head rises where men lack one"). Each new free city is a power with a seat of its own, by the rules of item 11+. Built after item 13, since it needs governors and commanders, and after 11b's risen heads. Split from the city-states item on 21 October 2026, when city-states as powers moved forward to item 11+; a vassal who stops paying is free in practice already there. With revolt comes the gate opened from within, when a besieged city's hunger breaks its loyalty ("How long a siege lasts"). And an army living off the land angers its people (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "An army eating from the actual citizens stores then should make them pretty unhappy?", and to the design session's takes, "Yes, to all, expertly!"): troops taking food raise unrest by how much they take, their own king's included; every province carries unrest, the homeland too, though absorbed land starts loyal and needs far more to rise; each army buys its food where it stands by leave or takes it, as its king's order says once it arrives, but by need when it has no gold to buy with, and by its commander's choice once it has one, who may keep the gold sent for food and take anyway (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "But remember, when you say a king decides how his army supplies himself. Information time travel stoll applies. He can tell them to buy, but if he hasn't sent them enough money to buy with, they will do what they must to eat. And an army with an assigned commander (a character) the commander has the final say on following orders or not. He may keep any money meant for food, and just take instead."); and a ruler whose land was taken from remembers it as a grievance ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice" under War, "Armies need food as well as pay" under Land, people and economy). The script kings weigh buying against taking, and the item's report shows how often each is chosen and how often a homeland province rose. And the age is lengthened, set now rather than in item 18 since every later measurement reads the end of the age (Haakon, 30 October 2026: "Yes to 1."): the ending's median from 44 to about 80 seasons and the cap from 80 to 100 to 140 to 160 ("Random ending" under Victory), the omens' darkest tier at season 140; the report shows game lengths and in how many ages a Great King's war was decided (a Great King's capital taken or a Great King made another's vassal), before and after, with a new save version. Then **17+, the opening as it stood, and the land east of the Jordan** (30 October 2026; after item 17, before item 18, one more save version): each army and fleet starts where the sources place it in 1346 (garrisons, field forces, occupiers), and each documented debt between courts starts on record, both from the dossiers with their grades ("Starting positions come from the sources" under The world); no letters or memories are written for any court. And the lands east of the Jordan go by the best-sourced reading (Haakon: "Is this the best read we have of the historical sources? If so, then i approve!"): the Shasu hold Seir (the later Edom) and the desert west of it (the later Negev), where Egypt's lists place them \[A\]; the Bashan is Ashtaroth's hinterland and the land south of it (the later Gilead) Pella's \[B\]; the plateau east of the Salt Sea, where Moab and Ammon rose centuries later, is land outside the game labelled by description, since neither name was yet in use (Haakon, 30 October 2026: "Agreed to all, expertly!"), so the Shasu no longer border Ashtaroth, Pella or Jerusalem (item 11f+'s guess, grade G, undone), the connections following the map's neighbours as 11f+ set them. And every place takes its own name ("Places by their own names" under The world; Haakon, 30 October 2026: "Agreed to all, expertly!"): the map, the seat view, every request, report and chronicle show the name the sources of 1346 use (Dimashqa, Gubla, Pihil, Urusalim), each checked against the dossiers and graded, a place with no attested name of the period labelled by description, the modern name on a second line of the province card and in the rulebook's gazetteer; the engine's ids stay as they are; and only what stood in 1346 is drawn as standing ("Places by their own names"): Shuwardata's land centred on Gath, not Hebron, and Nesa a land with no great town; and every town's people as it stood in 1346, not at its height (Haakon: "All that was materially, we should represent as accurate as possible"): Akhetaten, still being built, at about 15,000 to 20,000, below Thebes and Memphis; Kalavasos, small and new, about 1,000; Nesa about 1,000; Gath, in Hebron's place, a town of several thousand; Tunip, its site not securely found, about 4,000 to 5,000 beside Niya and Qadesh (Haakon, 30 October 2026: "Agreed to all, expertly!", to the design session's check of all seventy towns, the rest within their dossiers' ranges); each checked against its dossier. The benchmarks before and after. Then **17++, what a king can count** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "Yes to both"): the province card shows a province's town and its land apart ("about 18,000 in the town; about 650,000 on its land"), as the engine already keeps them (the town's mouths eat from its market and empty its stores in a siege; the land's people harvest, pay tax and give levies), so a capital's card no longer reads as a city of 645,350; and every count a king or a model sees is as his scribes could know it, his people as well as his last count's age allows ("Counts as the scribes knew them" under The world), the engine and god view exact; and the census ("A census" under The world; Haakon, 30 October 2026: "Agreed to all!"): scribes sent to count a province, paid and taking seasons, their count travelling home dated; a counted province pays its full tax, levy and work gangs, an uncounted one hides a share growing with the years since its count and its distance from the capital; counting stirs some unrest; and the king says how much he wants ("The king says how much he wants" under The world): grain as a share or an amount, levy and work gangs as a number of men, the burden falling on the people really there, so an amount or a levy set from a stale count squeezes the survivors (a smaller next harvest, hunger, unrest, flight) unless he asks for less or counts again. Script kings use the census and judge their demands by their counts where it pays, measured against scripts that never count. **Stop for review.**
